text: The Reliability pillar encompasses the ability of a workload to perform its intended function correctly and consistently when it is expected to. A resilient workload recovers quickly from failures to meet business and customer demand.

Foundational requirements extend beyond a single workload. Before architecting any system, ensure you have sufficient network bandwidth between your data centers and the cloud. AWS provides service quotas, also called limits, that cap how much of a resource you can provision.

Change management is how you monitor and respond to changes in demand. Failure management includes backing up data, designing for fault isolation across Availability Zones, and planning for disaster recovery so a workload can recover after an outage.

The Security pillar describes how to protect data, systems, and assets. Implement a strong identity foundation with least-privilege access, enable traceability by monitoring and logging actions, and apply security at all layers of the architecture.

Detection lets you identify a potential security misconfiguration, threat, or unexpected behavior. Configure logging, metrics, and alerts so that you can investigate and respond. Monitoring is also central to operational health, not only security.

The Performance Efficiency pillar focuses on using computing resources efficiently to meet requirements and maintaining that efficiency as demand changes. Select the right resource types and sizes, and monitor performance to make informed decisions.

The Cost Optimization pillar is the ability to run systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point. Adopt a consumption model, measure overall efficiency, and stop spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting such as managing your own data centers.

The Operational Excellence pillar includes the ability to support development and run workloads effectively, gain insight into operations, and continuously improve supporting processes and procedures. Perform operations as code and make frequent, small, reversible changes.

Disaster recovery strategies range from backup and restore, through pilot light and warm standby, to multi-site active-active. Each strategy trades off recovery time objective and recovery point objective against cost and operational complexity.

Elasticity is the ability to acquire resources as you need them and release them when you no longer need them. Automatic scaling responds to changes in demand, improving both reliability under load and cost efficiency during quiet periods.
